question: Which statement best describes Element selector?
options: A class selector begins with a dot, such as `.card`, and matches elements with that class. One class can be reused on many cards. It is like a shared membership label. Classes are the usual choice for reusable component styles because they describe a role without requiring a unique element.

A descendant selector uses a space to match an element inside another, such as `.menu a` for links inside a menu. It is like giving an instruction to items in one area. Keep selector chains short; a long chain can break when the markup structure changes.

An element selector uses a tag name, such as `p`, to match paragraph elements. It is like addressing everyone with the same role. Use it for broad defaults, such as base text styles, and use component classes when different areas need distinct appearances.

An ID selector begins with `#`, such as `#main`, and matches an element with that ID. An ID should be unique on the page. It is like addressing one specific person. IDs are useful for anchors and scripting, while reusable visual styles usually belong in classes.
explanation: An element selector uses a tag name, such as `p`, to match paragraph elements. It is like addressing everyone with the same role. Use it for broad defaults, such as base text styles, and use component classes when different areas need distinct appearances.

question: Which statement best describes Class selector?
options: Specificity helps determine which matching rule wins when rules set the same property. IDs generally outweigh classes, and classes generally outweigh element names; source order resolves some ties. It is like a priority system for competing instructions. Prefer simple selectors so overrides remain predictable.
